summary:
AnalogFit is an open web map that screens Earth locations as analogs for three reference
sites: the lunar south pole, the Mare Tranquillitatis pit, and Arcadia Planitia on Mars. It does not ask
whether a place looks like the Moon or Mars. It asks whether the place matches for one specific test,
such as rover navigation, landing hazard detection, or resource extraction. For each Earth site, target
and test, AnalogFit computes a similarity index only from features that are measured in a comparable
way on both worlds, lowers the index for Earth-only conditions such as rainfall, and reports how
much of the evidence the test needs is covered. This version compares 500 m terrain slope from
NASA LOLA and MOLA with NASA SRTM/ASTER and Copernicus GLO-30 elevation at 599
Earth locations, adds modeled low-Sun lighting, and uses NASA POWER climate data. Every number
traces to an archived, checksummed source file. Features without comparable data on both worlds are
shown as missing and are never guessed. Analog choice decides whether a field test means anything,
so the tool shows both where an analog fits and where the evidence stops.
details: What exactly does it do? AnalogFit is an interactive 2D map and 3D globe. The user chooses a target and a test type, and the tool ranks Earth locations for that combination. Selecting a location opens a dossier with its similarity index, its evidence coverage, the Earth and target values side by side, the data sources, a 3D terrain view, dated NASA imagery, and the stated limits of the comparison. Targets: T1, a lunar south-polar reference patch (89.6° S); T2, the surface beside the Mare Tranquillitatis pit (8.34° N, 33.22° E); T3, a patch of Arcadia Planitia, Mars (45° N, 200° E). Test types (10): landing hazard detection, landing plume and touchdown, navigation, mobility, robotics, construction, in situ resource utilization (ISRU), thermal and hardware endurance, human operations procedures, and suit and physiology. Earth locations (599): 585 global land samples, 7 well-known analog sites, 4 hypothesis sites (Kunene anorthosite complex, Mount Howe, a blocky lava field, Harrat Khaybar), and 3 rainforest negative controls. How does it work? 1. An analog is a triple: an Earth site, a target, and a test. A site can suit one test and fail another, so every score is specific to the test. 2. Evidence rule. A feature enters the score only if it is supported on both Earth and the target at a matched scale. In this version that feature is terrain slope, computed the same way on both worlds: the median of four gradients on a 3 by 3 grid with a 500 m baseline over a patch of about 1 km. Low-Sun lighting comes from an idealized solar-geometry model and is labeled as modeled. 3. Score. Each feature gets a Gaussian similarity to the target value. The features are combined with a weighted geometric mean, so one bad mismatch cannot be hidden by a good match elsewhere. The result is multiplied by a penalty for Earth-only contamination, currently annual rainfall from NASA POWER (2001 to 2025 climatology). The index runs from 0 to 100. It is a screening index, not a probability of mission success. 4. Coverage. Next to every score the tool shows the share of the test's total weight that is supported by data. Mineralogy, grain size, radar, ground ice, dust, and local target temperature are not yet comparable on both worlds, so they count as missing. Missing data is never treated as zero and never filled in. 5. Sensitivity. A Monte Carlo run (1,000 draws) varies the weights and tolerances and reports the range of each score. The range shows sensitivity to our assumptions. It is not a measurement confidence interval. 6. Physics that Earth cannot copy. Gravity, atmospheric pressure, and radiation differ on Earth for every site. The tool explains this for each test in plain words, for example that engine-plume tests behave very differently without air and under low gravity. 7. Provenance. The audit verifies 680 original source files by SHA-256 checksum and decodes the planetary elevations again from the archived NASA PDS bytes. Each dossier can export an evidence card with sources and checksums. What did the tests show? We report the results as they are. Of 14 documented roles of known analog sites, 3 can be tested with the data now in the score, and none of the 3 pass our threshold (coverage of at least 50%, score of at least 50, and rank in the top 5% of global samples). Two simple baseline methods also pass 0 of 3, so this version does not yet show an advantage over a simple distance measure. The rainforest negative controls are rejected in 81 of 90 comparisons, with 9 untestable and none wrongly accepted. That rejection is driven mostly by rainfall. This version is therefore an audited prototype, not a validated site selector. We did not tune weights to make the validation pass. What benefits does it have? It replaces looks-like judgments with a comparison that names the test, the features, and the data behind each number. It shows how much evidence supports a score, so a high score with thin evidence cannot be mistaken for a strong match. It keeps failed and untestable results visible. Anyone can rerun the pipeline, check the checksums, and reproduce the scores. What do you hope to achieve? We want to add features that are comparable on both worlds, in this order: target temperature from LRO Diviner and Mars TES/THEMIS matched to quality-screened MODIS land surface temperature; mineralogy; ground ice; and radar roughness. We want to replace the single reference patches with fixed target regions, estimate measurement uncertainty, and then repeat the validation against known analog sites. Only after it passes would we search for new analog sites and present them as discoveries. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? Python (NumPy, pandas, requests, rasterio, Pillow) for data download, feature computation, scoring, audit, and reports. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the web application, with Leaflet 1.9.4 for the map and globe.gl for the 3D globe, both bundled locally. Playwright with Chrome for automated browser tests, which compare the Python and browser scores across 35,940 values. LaTeX for the paper. Hardware: personal laptops only. Use of AI Tools used: Claude (Anthropic) and OpenAI Codex. Where and how: these tools helped draft and edit the text of the paper and of this document, and helped write, review, and test the Python and JavaScript code. The AnalogFit logo, the intro animation, and the Moon and Mars shown in the intro are drawn by code written with this assistance. They are illustrations, not mission data. All scores come from our Python scripts running on data downloaded from the sources listed below. No tool generated or altered data values. The project does not use, contain, or modify NASA logos, flags, or mission identifiers. The use of these tools is also stated in the project README.
